﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾. The meaning of *subḥān* (Glory; exalted above all imperfection) is *tanazzuh* (transcendence above imperfection). It is a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) that is *ghayr munṣarif* (indeclinable). *Asrā* and *sarā* are two dialectal forms meaning "to travel by night." The verb is intransitive (*ghayr muta'addin*). Ibn 'Aṭiyya chose to read *asrā* here as transitive, meaning that the angels took His servant by night, but this is far-fetched. The "servant" here is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). He is described with servanthood only to honour him and bring him near.

*Laylan* (by night). If it is asked: what is the benefit of saying *laylan* when travelling by night is already implied? The answer is that by using the indefinite form, *laylan*, He intended to indicate that the duration of the journey was short, and that he was taken by night for only part of it, although the distance was that of forty nights' travel. This is more striking as a wonder.

﴿From the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾. By the Sacred Mosque is meant the Mosque of Makkah that surrounds the Ka'bah. It has been narrated in a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was sleeping in al-Hijr, Jibril came to me." It is also said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was in his house on the night of the Isra', so that according to this view the Sacred Mosque means Makkah, that is, the city of the Sacred Mosque. As for the Farthest Mosque, it is Bayt al-Maqdis, which is in Iliya'. It was called "the Farthest" because there was no mosque beyond it at that time. It is also possible that by "the Farthest" he meant "the most distant," so the purpose would be to show the wonder of traveling in one night to this distant place.

The scholars differed about the manner of the Isra'. The majority said it was with the body and the spirit of the Prophet (ﷺ). Some people said it was with his spirit alone, and that it was a true dream. The proof of the majority is that if it had been a dream, Quraysh would not have denied it, and there would have been nothing with which the disbelievers could call him a liar. Do you not see the words of Umm Hani' to him: "Do not tell anyone about this, or your people will call you a liar." The proof of those who said the Isra' was a dream is the saying of the Exalted: "And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people." The word *ru'yā* is used for what is seen in sleep, and it is also used for what is seen with the eyes. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was between sleeping and waking," and he mentioned the Isra'. At the end of the hadith he said: "Then I awoke and I was in the Sacred Mosque."

Some people reconciled the evidences and said: the Isra' happened twice, once with the body and once with the spirit. The Isra' with the body was from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is what Quraysh denied. The Isra' with the spirit was to the seven heavens, on the night the five prayers were enjoined, and he met the prophets in the heavens.

﴿The one whose surroundings We have blessed﴾: this is a description of the Farthest Mosque. Its blessing extends to its surroundings in two ways: first, what was in it and in its regions of prophets; second, the abundance of crops and trees in it, which Allah specially favoured al-Sham (Greater Syria) with.

﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾: that is, that We might show Muhammad (ﷺ) on that night some of the wonders. He saw the heavens, Paradise, Hell, Sidrat al-Muntaha, the angels and the prophets, and Allah spoke to him, as is related in the hadiths of the Isra', which are in the books of hadith. Their mention is therefore dispensed with here.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 2–3:

﴿And We made it a guidance﴾ It may be that the pronoun refers to the Book, or to Musa (Moses). ﴿That you not take, other than Me, a guardian﴾ That is, a lord to whom you entrust your affairs. It may also be that the "an" (that) is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) or an explanatory particle (mufassirah). ﴿O descendants of those whom We carried with Nuh (Noah)﴾ This is a vocative address. In addressing them thus there is gentleness and a reminder of God's blessing. It has also been said that it is the object of "tattakhidhu" (you take), and the meaning is made definite by the reading of the one who reads "yattakhidh" with the ya' (third person), and "those whom We carried with Nuh" means his three sons, who are Sam, Ham and Yafith, and their wives, and from them the people multiplied after the Flood. ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ That is, he was greatly thankful; he would praise God in every state. This is a reason for what was mentioned before, that is, be grateful as your father Nuh was grateful.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 4–6:

﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book﴾. It is said: here "qadayna" means "We made known and informed," as it was said in ﴿And We conveyed to him that matter﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. On this reading, "the Book" is the Torah. It is also said: "qadayna ilayhi" means "We decreed" in the sense of qada' and qadar, and on this reading "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in which the measures of all things were written. Here "ila" carries the sense of "ala" (upon). ﴿You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice﴾. This sentence explains what was decreed. If "qadayna" is taken in the sense of qada' and qadar, the sentence stands in the position of the answer (jawab) to "qadayna," since it follows the pattern of an oath. If it is taken in the sense of "a'lamna" (We informed), then it is the answer to an implied oath, its sense being: "By God, you will surely corrupt," and the sentence is in the position of the object (ma'mul) of "qadayna." The two occasions referred to are: first, the killing of Zakariyya, and second, the killing of Yahya, peace be upon them both. ﴿And you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾. "Ulu" (exaltation) means arrogance and self-conceit. ﴿So when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent against you servants of Ours﴾. Its meaning: when they corrupted the first time, God sent against them His servants to take vengeance upon them through their hands. Scholars differed about who these servants were. It is said they were Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers, and the killing by Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon. ﴿So they went through the homes, searching,﴾ that is, they roamed among them with corruption. It is narrated that they killed their scholars, burned the Torah, destroyed the mosques, and took captive seventy thousand of them. ﴿Then We gave you back the turn against them﴾, that is, dominion and victory over those who were sent against you; it refers to the return of kingship to the Children of Israel and the rescue of their captives. It is said this was after Bukhtnassar, and it is also said it was the killing of Jalut by Dawud (David). ﴿with more manpower (nafir)﴾, that is, greater in number. It is a verbal noun from your saying "nafara al-rajul," meaning the man went out hastily, or it is the plural of "nafar."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 7:

﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾ The first "ahsantum" carries the sense of "good deeds" (al-hasanat), and the second carries the sense of "kindness" (al-ihsan), as in your saying: "ahsantu ila fulan" (I was kind to so-and-so). So there is here a tajnis (paronomasia), and the lam in it carries the meaning of "ila" (to). Similarly is the lam in His words: "And if you do evil, it is for them" ﴿فَإِذَا جَآءَ وَعْدُ ٱلآخِرَةِ لِيَسُوءُواْ وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ [So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to disgrace your faces]: meaning, when they (the Israelites) corrupted in the last instance, God sent against them those servants of His to take vengeance upon them. So "al-akhirah" is an attribute of "al-marrah" (the occasion). The meaning of "yasu'u" is: they make the traces of evil and ugliness appear in them, as in His words: "their faces were made to look evil (suyyithat wujuh alladhina kafaru)". The lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and it is connected to the omitted "ba'atha" (We sent), which is indicated by the first. It has also been said that it is the lam of command. ﴿وَلِيَدْخُلُواْ ٱلْمَسْجِدَ﴾ [And that they might enter the Masjid], meaning Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿وَلِيُتَبِّرُواْ﴾ [And that they might destroy completely], from "al-tabar", which is destruction and extreme corruption. ﴿مَا عَلَوْاْ﴾ [what they had conquered]: "ma" is the object of "yutabbiru": that is, they destroy what they had gained dominion over of the lands. It has also been said that "ma" is temporal, meaning they corrupt for the duration of their domination.

ﷻ"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you." Addressed to the Children of Israel; its meaning is a hope of mercy for them if they repent after the second corruption. ﴿And if you return, We will return.﴾ Addressed to the Children of Israel: that is, if you return to corruption, We will return to punishing you. And they did return, so God sent against them Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, who would kill them and humiliate them until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿A prison.﴾ That is, a confinement, and it derives from the root ḥ-ṣ-r (to confine). It has also been said that it means something spread out and laid down, like the well-known reed mat (ḥaṣīr).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 9–11:

﴿It guides to that which is most upright﴾. That is, the way and the condition which are most upright. It has also been said: it means "There is no god but Allah," though the wording is more general than that.

﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾. The meaning is censure and reproach for what people do in anger, namely invoking curses upon themselves, their wealth and their children. They call for evil at that time just as they call for good at times of tranquility. It has also been said that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and it has already been mentioned that the correct view regarding the one who said it is that it was Abu Jahl.

﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾. Here, and in the verse before it, "al-insan" (man) is a generic noun (ism jins). It has also been said that here it refers to Adam, but this is far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 12:

﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾. There are two interpretations. The first: that the night and the day are two signs in themselves, so the idafa (construct phrase) in "the sign of the night" and "the sign of the day" is like your saying "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque), meaning the sign which is the night and the sign which is the day. On this view, the effacing of the sign of the night is its being dark. The second interpretation: that by the sign of the night is meant the moon, and by the sign of the day is meant the sun. On this view, the effacing of the sign of the night is the moon not being given the light of the sun. ﴿And We made the sign of the day to be seeing﴾. It may mean the day itself or the sun, and the meaning of "mubsira" (seeing, giving sight) is that things are seen by it. ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, i.e., that you may use the light of the day to reach the pursuit of your livelihoods. ﴿And that you may know﴾ by the alternation of night and day, or by the movement of the sun and the moon, ﴿the number of years and the reckoning﴾, i.e., the months and the days. ﴿And every thing We have detailed with full detail﴾. "Kull" (every) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, and "tafsil" (detailing) means clarification.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 13–14:

﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (his deeds) to his neck﴾. "Kull" (every) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb. "Ṭā'ir" (bird) here means his deed, and the meaning is that his deed is bound to him. It is also said: "his bird" is what has been decreed for him, both good and evil, and according to this meaning, whatever a person encounters has already been preceded by divine decree. It is expressed by "bird" because the Arabs used to take omens of good fortune and misfortune from birds (tayammun and tashā'um). His saying "around his neck" means that it is like a necklace or a shackle that does not part from him. ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record that he will find spread open﴾, meaning the book of his deeds, containing his good deeds and evil deeds. ﴿Read your record! Sufficient is yourself today against you as a reckoner﴾. Its implied sense is that it will be said to him: "Read!" ﴿Ḥasīban﴾ means "one who reckons," or it derives from ḥisāb in the sense of counting.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 15:

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.﴾ Its meaning, wherever it occurs, is that no one is held accountable for the sin of another. Al-wizr (burden) in the lexicon means weight and load, and it is intended here to mean sins. The meaning of "tazir" (bears) is that one carries the burden of another, i.e., the burden of another soul. ﴿And We would never punish until We had sent a messenger.﴾ It has been said: this pertains to the ruling of this world, meaning that God does not destroy a community except after giving them warning by sending them a messenger. It has also been said: it is general to this world and the Hereafter, and that God does not punish a people in the Hereafter unless He had sent to them a messenger, and they disbelieved in him and disobeyed him. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Every time a company is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did no warner come to you?" They will say, "Yes..."﴾ [al-Mulk: 8-9]. From this is derived the ruling concerning the people of fatra (the interval between messengers). The Ahl al-Sunnah (People of the Sunnah) used this verse to establish that moral obligation (taklif) binds servants only through revelation (al-shar'), not through reason alone.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 16–17:

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein﴾ There are three interpretations of "amarna" (We commanded) here. The first: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its meaning being: We commanded its affluent ones to do good and obedience, but they disobeyed and transgressed. The second: "amarna" is an expression for decreeing judgment upon them with transgression, i.e., We decreed upon them, so they transgressed. The third: "amarna" means "We multiplied," and this is the view chosen by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for the reading "ami'arna" with a lengthened hamza, it means "We multiplied." As for the reading "ammarna" with a doubled mim, it is from imara (command/rule), i.e., We made them rulers, so they transgressed. "Mutraf" (affluent one) means the wealthy and pampered person in this world. ﴿So the word came to be fulfilled against it﴾, i.e., the decree that Allah had decreed. ﴿And how many generations We have destroyed after Noah﴾ A "qarn" (generation) is a hundred years; it is also said to be forty.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 18–22:

﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life of this world)﴾ (verse): This is about the disbelievers who desire the worldly life and do not believe in the Hereafter, although its wording is more general than that. The meaning is that Allah hastens for them a share of this world under two restrictions: first, restricting the amount hastened to the will of Allah; and second, restricting the person to whom it is hastened to the will of Allah. ﴿for whomever We will﴾ is a substitute for ﴿for whom﴾, and it is a substitute of part from whole. ﴿Rejected﴾ means driven away or humiliated. ﴿And strives for it its striving﴾ means he works for it its work. ﴿Each (group) We provide with aid﴾: "each" is in the accusative governed by "We provide," which is from "madad" (providing increase), and its meaning is: We increase them from Our bounty. ﴿These and those﴾ is a substitute for "each," and the indication is to the two groups mentioned before. ﴿From the bounty of your Lord﴾ means the provision of this world. It was said: it means from acts of obedience for those who desire the Hereafter, and from acts of disobedience for those who desire this world; but the first is more apparent. ﴿Restricted﴾ means prevented. ﴿We have preferred some of them﴾ means in worldly provision. ﴿Do not make﴾ is addressed to a single person, but what is meant is all of creation, because the addressee is not specified. ﴿Blameworthy﴾ means that Allah and the best of His servants blame him. ﴿Forsaken﴾ means unsupported.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 18–22:

﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life of this world)﴾ (verse): This is about the disbelievers who desire the worldly life and do not believe in the Hereafter, although its wording is more general than that. The meaning is that Allah hastens for them a share of this world under two restrictions: first, restricting the amount hastened to the will of Allah; and second, restricting the person to whom it is hastened to the will of Allah. ﴿for whomever We will﴾ is a substitute for ﴿for whom﴾, and it is a substitute of part from whole. ﴿Rejected﴾ means driven away or humiliated. ﴿And strives for it its striving﴾ means he works for it its work. ﴿Each (group) We provide with aid﴾: "each" is in the accusative governed by "We provide," which is from "madad" (providing increase), and its meaning is: We increase them from Our bounty. ﴿These and those﴾ is a substitute for "each," and the indication is to the two groups mentioned before. ﴿From the bounty of your Lord﴾ means the provision of this world. It was said: it means from acts of obedience for those who desire the Hereafter, and from acts of disobedience for those who desire this world; but the first is more apparent. ﴿Restricted﴾ means prevented. ﴿We have preferred some of them﴾ means in worldly provision. ﴿Do not make﴾ is addressed to a single person, but what is meant is all of creation, because the addressee is not specified. ﴿Blameworthy﴾ means that Allah and the best of His servants blame him. ﴿Forsaken﴾ means unsupported.

**"And your Lord has decreed"** means He judged, obligated, and required. It may also mean He commanded. This is supported by the reading in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "And your Lord has enjoined" (﴿ووصى ربك﴾). **"That you worship not"** (﴿ألا تعبدوا﴾): *an* (أن) here is either *mufassira* (explanatory) or *masdariyya* (verbal), with the sense "that you do not worship." **"If one or both of them reach old age with you"** (﴿إما يبلغن عندك﴾): this is *in* (إن) the conditional particle, to which *ma* (ما), the emphatic particle, has been attached. Its response is **"then do not say to them, 'Uff'"** (﴿فلا تقل لهما أف﴾). The meaning is an injunction to honour one's parents when they grow old, or when one of them does. Old age is singled out because at that stage they are most in need of kindness and of having their rights fulfilled, due to their weakness. **"With you"** (عندك) means in your house and under your care.

**"Uff"** (أف): wherever it occurs, it is a verb-noun (*ism fi'l*), and its meaning is an expression of displeasure. It is said in irritation and the like. What is intended by it is the least disagreeable word that can come from a person. God, exalted is He, forbade that this be said to one's parents. Therefore it is all the more fitting and deserving that nothing beyond it be said to them. *Uff* may be pronounced with a kasra, a fatha, or a damma. These are vowels of fixed ending (*harakat bina'*). As for its *tanwin* (nunation), it marks indefiniteness (*lil-tankir*).

**"And do not scold them"** (﴿ولا تنهرهما﴾): from *al-intihar*, which is harshness in speech.

**"And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy"** (﴿واخفض لهما جناح الذل من الرحمة﴾): this is a metaphor for humility towards them and gentleness with them. Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 26–28:

﴿And give the kinsman his due﴾. This is addressed to all people, for the sake of maintaining kinship ties and showing kindness to them. It was also said that it is a address specific to the Prophet ﷺ, that he should give his relatives their due from the public treasury (bayt al-mal), but the first view is more preferred.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ – the verse means: if you turn away from the kinsmen, the needy and the wayfarer, when you do not find anything to give them, then speak to them a gentle word. The Prophet ﷺ, when someone asked him and he had nothing to give, would turn away from him out of modesty, so he was commanded to use good speech in that case, namely to say: "May Allah provide for you," "May Allah give you," or something similar. The word maysur (﴿مَّيْسُوراً﴾, "gentle") is derived from yusr (ease).

﴿seeking mercy from your Lord, which you hope for﴾ – this is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It may be connected to the phrase ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, and the meaning according to this is that he turns away from them while waiting for a provision to come to him, so that he may give it to them; the "mercy" in this case is the provision he hopes for. Or it may be connected to the phrase ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, meaning: seek your Lord's mercy with gentle speech; and the "mercy" in this case is the reward and recompense.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 29–30:

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ (a metaphor for the utmost stinginess; as if the miser's hand were held back from giving and tied to his neck). ﴿And do not extend it with complete extension﴾ (a metaphor for the utmost generosity). So God forbade both extremes and commanded moderation between them, like His saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. ﴿Blameworthy﴾, meaning your friend will blame you for excessive giving and for harming yourself; or those deserving of giving will blame you, because you have left nothing to give; or all people will blame you for wastefulness in giving. ﴿Depleted﴾, meaning cut off with nothing left with you, and it is from the expression "ḥasira al-safar al-baʿīr" (the journey exhausted the camel), when it wearies it until it has no strength left. ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, meaning He widens it for whom He wills and narrows it for whom He wills, so do not be concerned by what you see of that, for God knows best the interests of His servants.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 31–33:

﴿And do not kill your children﴾ This was mentioned in al-An'am (al-An'am [151]). ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ The right that makes killing a soul lawful is what is related in the hadith, from his saying (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man may not be shed except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, adultery after having been married, or killing another soul." Other things are connected to these, because they are similar in meaning, such as banditry (hirabah), abandoning the prayer, and withholding the zakat. ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ The "wronged" (mazlum) here is the one killed without right. The "heir" (wali) is the heir of the one killed and the whole body of male relatives (asabah); according to Malik, women are not among the heirs. The "authority" (sultan) that Allah has given him is: retaliation (qisas), or the choice between pardon and retaliation. ﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾ This is a prohibition against the heir of the one killed exceeding the bounds, by killing someone other than the killer, or killing two for one, or other forms of transgression. It has been read as "fa-la tusrif" with the ta' (addressing the killer, or the heir of the one killed). ﴿Indeed, he is ever supported﴾ The pronoun refers to the one killed or to his heir, and his support is retaliation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 34–35:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. It was mentioned in al-An'am [6:152]. Some of them said: "Do not approach" and "do not kill" are conjoined to "that you not worship" (an alla ta'budu). The apparent reading is that they are in the jussive mood by the prohibition, as evidenced by His saying after them: ﴿and do not stalk about (wa la taqfu) and do not walk (wa la tamshi)﴾. It is also valid that they be conjoined (ma'tufat) if we make "an alla ta'budu" jussive upon the prohibition, with "an" being explanatory (mufassirah). ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾: it is general concerning covenants with Allah and with people. ﴿Indeed, the covenant is ever [that about which one will be] questioned﴾: it may have two meanings. One: that it carries the sense of a demand, i.e., it is required that it be fulfilled. The second: that the meaning is that it will be questioned about on the Day of Resurrection, whether it was fulfilled or not. ﴿And weigh with an even balance (al-qistas)﴾: it was said: al-qistas is the balance, and it was said: justice. It was also read with a kasra on the qaf, and this is a dialect (lughah). ﴿And better in result (ta'wil)﴾: i.e., better in outcome and final destination, and it derives from "alla," meaning "to return."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 36:

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. The meaning: do not say what you do not know, such as disparaging people and the like. The word is derived from "qafawtu" (qafawtu), meaning I followed it, i.e., I pursued it.

﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about﴾. "Those" (ulaika) refers to the hearing, the sight, and the heart. He treated them in the manner of rational beings in using the demonstrative "those," because they are faculties that have perception. The pronoun in "about it" (anhu) refers back to "all" (kullu), and "about it" is connected to "questioned" (mas'ulan). The meaning: a person will be questioned about his hearing, his sight, and his heart. It has also been said that the pronoun refers back to "that of which you have no knowledge," and the meaning according to this is that the hearing, the sight, and the heart are what will be questioned about what they have no knowledge of. This view is far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 37:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly.﴾ Al-maraḥ (arrogance, haughtiness) is conceit and pride in one's gait. It has also been said that it is excessive joy in this world. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal). ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth.﴾ That is, you will never make a rent in it by your walking upon it. Al-kharq is al-qaṭʿ (cutting through). It has also been said that its meaning is: you cannot traverse all of it by walking. The purpose of this is to give the reason for the prohibition of pride and haughtiness, meaning: if you, O human, cannot tear through the earth, nor reach the mountains in height, then how can you be proud and strut in your walking? Rather, what is obligatory upon you is humility.

﴿All that was its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.﴾ The reference is to the prohibited matters mentioned earlier. Here, *makruh* (hateful) means *haram* (forbidden), not in the technical sense used by the jurists (*fuqaha'*), who treat *makruh* as below *haram*. As for its grammatical analysis, *makruhan* is either an adjective (*na't*) of *sayyi'uhu*, or a substitute (*badal*) for it, or a second predicate (*khabar thani*) of *kana*.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 40:

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons⁠—﴾ This is an address in the form of rebuke to the Arabs who said, "The angels are daughters of Allah." The meaning is: How can He assign to you the superior part of offspring, which is males, while taking for Himself the inferior, which is daughters? The meaning of "asfākum" (favoured you) is: He singled you out for them. ﴿A tremendous saying﴾, i.e., of great abhorrence and monstrosity.

This is an argument for God's oneness, and it has two interpretations. The first: the meaning is that if there were other gods with God, they would have sought a way to draw near to Him through worship and obedience, and so they would be among His servants. The second: they would have sought a way to corrupt His dominion and to contend with Him in His power. It is known that this did not happen, so there is no god but Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 43–45:

﴿The seven heavens and the earth glorify Him﴾ — the verse: There is disagreement concerning the manner of this glorification. It has been said: it is glorification by the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal), meaning by what their craftsmanship indicates of power and wisdom. It has also been said: it is genuine glorification, and this is more preferable on account of His saying: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾. ﴿We have placed between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a veil, concealed﴾. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: that Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ that He would conceal him from the disbelievers when they intended him harm, and would shield him from them. The second: that He would veil the disbelievers from understanding the Qur'an, and this is more preferable on account of what follows it. As for "concealed" (mastur) here, it has been said that its meaning is: hidden from the eyes of creation, because it is part of Allah's subtle grace and sufficiency, and so it belongs to the unseen. It has also been said that its meaning is: veiling (satir).

﴿Veils (akinnah), lest they understand it﴾. Akinnah is the plural of kinan, which means a covering. "Lest they understand it" is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), its estimated meaning being: out of aversion that they understand it. These are metaphors for their misguidance.

﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 48–51:

﴿Behold how they coin comparisons for you﴾, that is, they liken you to the sorcerer, the poet, and the madman, ﴿so they have gone astray﴾ from the truth, ﴿and they cannot find a way﴾ to guidance. The verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions among the disbelievers. ﴿And they say: "When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be raised up as a new creation?"﴾ The meaning of the verse is a denial of resurrection and their deeming it unlikely that Allah would create them anew after their annihilation. Al-rufat is that which has decayed until it became dust or fine particles. The difference of the readers regarding the two interrogative particles has been mentioned in Surat al-Ra'd [13:5]. ﴿Say: "Be you stones or iron"﴾. The meaning: if you were stones or iron, We would still have power to resurrect and revive you, even though stones and iron are the hardest of things and the furthest from the moisture that is in life. So it is more fitting and more due that He resurrect your bodies and revive your decayed bones. The mention of stones and iron is a reminder, through them, of what is easier for life than them. The meaning of His saying "be" is: be in imagination and supposition, and it is not intended as a challenge to them, as some of them have said regarding it. ﴿Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾. It was said: it means the heavens, the earth and the mountains. It was also said: rather, it refers generally to their notions of whatever is great among them, that is: if you were stones or iron, or something greater in your estimation and further from life, We would still have power to resurrect you. ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾, that is, they will move them in the manner of one who deems a thing far-fetched and of one who mocks. ﴿And they say: "When will it be?"﴾, that is, when will the resurrection take place.

The commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 52:

﴿On the day He calls you, and you respond with His praise﴾ The "calling" here refers to the resurrection through the blowing of the Trumpet (al-Sur), and the "responding" refers to their rising from the graves in obedience and submission. "With His praise" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (al-hal), meaning praising Him. It is also said that the meaning of "with His praise" is "by His command." ﴿And you will think that you remained but a little﴾ meaning, you remained in the world or in the graves.

"My servants" here refers to the believers. He commanded them to say to one another gentle and pleasing words. It is also said that they were to say it to the polytheists, and that it was then abrogated (naskh) by the sword. The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of يقولوا is like His saying ﴿يُقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ﴾ in Surah Ibrahim [14:31], where the verb is in the jussive mood as a response to the imperative, with the final nun dropped. This has already been mentioned.

﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Him.﴾ It was said: this refers to the angels. It was also said: Jesus, his mother, and Uzayr (Ezra). And it was said: a group of jinn whom the Arabs used to worship. The meaning is that they have no power to remove harm from you, so how can you worship them?

﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord﴾. The meaning is that those deities you call upon besides God seek nearness to God, hope for His mercy, and fear Him. So how can you worship them alongside Him?

The grammatical analysis (i'rab, the study of case endings and sentence structure) of ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (those): it is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). ﴿alladhīna yad'ūna﴾ (those who call upon) is a descriptive phrase modifying it, and ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ (they seek) is its khabar (predicate). The subject of ﴿yad'ūna﴾ is a pronoun referring to the disbelievers, while the subject of ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ refers to the worshipped deities. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿yad'ūna﴾ and ﴿yabtaghūna﴾ refers to the prophets mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others﴾.

﴿al-wasīlah﴾ (the means) is that by which one seeks nearness and closeness to God.

﴿ayyuhum aqrab﴾ (which of them is nearest) is a badal (substitution in apposition) for the pronoun in ﴿yabtaghūna﴾, meaning: he seeks the means who is nearer than them, so how much more so anyone else? Or it is taken to imply the meaning of "eagerly strive," so it is as if it was said: they eagerly strive to determine which of them will be nearer to God through diligence in obedience to Him. It is also possible that the meaning is that they seek means through whichever of them is nearest to God.

﴿maḥdhūran﴾ (feared) derives from ﴿al-ḥadhar﴾ (caution), which is fear.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 58:

﴿And there is not a city but We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection﴾ This statement may bear two meanings. The first is that it refers to death and annihilation, which is inevitable. The second is that it refers to a command from God that seizes the city all at once and destroys it. This second meaning is more apparent, because the first is known and does not require being informed of it. The destruction and punishment mentioned in the verse actually apply to the people of the cities, that is, "We will destroy its people or punish them." It is related that Mecca's destruction came through the Abyssinians, Medina's through hunger, Kufa's through the Turks, and al-Andalus's through horses. al-Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr was asked about Granada, and he said: "It was struck by punishment on the day the Muwahhidun (Almohads) were killed there during the uprising of Ibn Hud." As for the destruction of Cordoba, Seville, Toledo and others by the Romans (Christians) seizing them, [it is also written] ﴿in the Book as an inscription﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 59:

﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them.﴾ The signs (al-ayat) here means those that the disbelievers proposed. If they saw them and did not believe, Allah would destroy them. The occasion of the verse is that the Quraysh proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he turn al-Safa into gold for them. Allah informed them that He did not do so, lest they deny and thereby be destroyed. He expressed the abstention from doing this as "prevention" (al-man'), and "an nursil" (that We send) is in the accusative position (mawdi' nasb), while "an kadhdhaba" (that they denied) is in the nominative position (mawdi' raf'). Then He mentioned the she-camel of Thamud as a reminder of this, because they proposed it and it was the cause of their destruction. The meaning of "mubsira" (manifest) is clear and evident in its indication.

﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning.﴾ If by "the signs" here is meant the proposed ones, the meaning is that He sends them as a warning of immediate punishment, which is destruction. If by it is meant the miracles that were not proposed, the meaning is that He sends them as a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, so that the disbeliever may see them and believe. It was also said: the intended "signs" here are thunder, earthquakes, eclipses, and other frightening phenomena.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 17, verse 60:**

﴿And [remember] when We told you, "Indeed your Lord has encompassed the people."﴾ The meaning is: remember when We revealed to you that your Lord had encompassed Quraysh, meaning We gave you the good news of their being killed on the day of Badr. This is His saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs.﴾ [Al-Qamar: 45]. He said "encompassed" in the past tense though it had not yet occurred, to affirm it and to establish that it would certainly happen. It was also said: the meaning is that He encompassed the people in protecting you and defending you from them, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 67].

﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people.﴾ Scholars differed about this vision. It was said that it is the Night Journey (al-Isra'). Whoever says it took place while awake, then "vision" means sight with the eye. Whoever says it took place in a dream, then the vision was a dream, and the trial in this case is the disbelievers' denial of it and the apostasy of some Muslims at that time. It was also said that it is the Prophet's ﷺ dream in his sleep of the defeat of the disbelievers and their killing at Badr, and the trial in this case is Quraysh's denial of it. It was also said that he saw that he would enter Mecca, so he hastened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, but he was turned back from it, and some Muslims were tried by this. It was also said that he saw in a dream that the Banu Umayyah were climbing up his pulpit, and he was grieved by this.

﴿And the cursed tree in the Qur'an﴾: this means the tree of Zaqqum. It is conjoined to "the vision," meaning that Allah made the vision and the tree a trial for the people. That is because when Quraysh heard that there is a tree of Zaqqum in Hell, they mocked it and said: "How can there be a tree in the Fire when the Fire burns trees?" Abu Jahl said: "I know of zaqqum only as dates with butter." If it is asked: why was the tree of Zaqqum cursed in the Qur'an? The answer is that what is meant is the curse upon those who eat it. It was also said: the curse here means distance and removal, because it is at the root of Hellfire.

﴿And We warn them﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

﴿Transgression﴾ (ṭughyānan) is a tamyiz (a noun in the accusative specifying what is left ambiguous by the preceding verb) or a ḥāl (an accusative of circumstance describing the state of the subject), either from the pronoun in "من" or from the object of "خلقت" (as stated in the text).

"He said, 'Have you considered this one whom You have honoured over me?'" The kaf in "araytaka" (have you considered) is for address (al-khitab) and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The speech is abbreviated by omitting that part. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "araytaka hadha" means "have you considered" and the like, not "inform me."

"La-ahtanikanna dhurriyyatahu" means: "I will surely take control over them and lead them." It is derived from tahnik al-dabba (the halter of the animal), which is when a rope is tightened around its jaw so that it submits.

"He said, 'Go!'" Ibn 'Atiyya said: the imperative and what follows it of imperatives are in the form of a command but in the manner of a threat. Al-Zamakhshari said: the intended meaning is not the going that is the opposite of coming; rather it means: "Proceed to your affair that you have chosen," as abandonment of him and leaving him to himself. In my view it may also mean: dismissal and banishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 64:

﴿And incite﴾: i.e., deceive and lure. ﴿with your voice﴾: It is said that this means singing and musical instruments, and it is said that it means calling to acts of disobedience. ﴿And urge against them﴾: i.e., terrify them. It derives from *al-jalaba*, which is shouting. ﴿with your horse and your foot soldiers﴾: "Horse" here refers to the horsemen who ride horses, and "foot soldiers" is the plural of *rajil*, meaning one who walks on his feet. It is said that this is *majaz* (figurative usage) and *isti'ara* (metaphor), meaning: exert your utmost effort. It is also said that Satan has horses and foot soldiers. And it is said that the intended meaning is the horsemen and foot soldiers of mankind who act in evil. ﴿And share with them in wealth and children﴾: Sharing in wealth means acquiring it through *riba* (usury) and spending it on acts of disobedience and other things. Sharing in children is by fathering them through adultery, and by naming a child ʿAbd Shams, ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, and the like. ﴿And promise them﴾: i.e., false promises, such as the intercession of idols and the like.

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾ means the believers who put their trust in God. This is shown by His words that follow: "And your Lord is sufficient as Disposer of affairs," and by similar verses such as: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾ [An-Nahl: 99].

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 17, verses 66–67:

﴿It is He who drives the ship for you upon the sea﴾, i.e., makes it run and move; al-fulk here is a collective noun. (It is) in seeking His bounty through trade and other things. ﴿When harm touches you at sea﴾, meaning fear of drowning, ﴿those you invoke vanish, except Him﴾. Here "ḍalla" means to perish and be lost: that is, every one you call upon, other than God alone, has been lost from your imaginations and thoughts, so you turn to Him alone at that time, not to anyone else. So how can you worship other than Him, when in that hardship you find none but Him? ﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾, i.e., ungrateful for blessings. Here "al-insan" refers to the category of humankind.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 68–70:

﴿Do you feel secure﴾: The hamza is for reproach, and the fa' is for coordination. That is: you have been saved from the sea, so do you feel secure from being swallowed up by the land? ﴿a violent storm of stones (ḥāṣib)﴾: meaning stones, or a violent wind that hurls pebbles. ﴿an advocate (wakīl)﴾: that is, one who manages your affairs and helps you. ﴿a wind that breaks up what it encounters (qāṣif)﴾: that is, the one that shatters what it strikes, that is, breaks it. ﴿a pursuer (tabī')﴾: that is, one who demands from us an account of what we did to you; meaning, you will not find anyone among us to help you, like His saying ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾ [al-Shams: 15]. ﴿And We have favoured them above many of those We have created, with [marked] preference﴾: meaning, He favoured them over the jinn and over all other animals, but He did not favour them over the angels, which is why He said "over many." The kinds of preference are numerous and cannot be counted, and the exegetes have mentioned from them that man eats with his hand and that he stands erect; these are examples.

Translation:

﴿With their imam﴾. It is said: this means their prophet, as one says, "O followers of so-and-so" (ya ummat fulan). It is also said: it means their book that was revealed to them. And it is said: it means the book in which their deeds are recorded. ﴿And they will not be wronged even as much as the thread [in a date-stone]﴾. The fatil is the thread that lies in the split of a date-stone. The meaning is that they will not be wronged in their deeds, neither a little nor a lot; He mentions the smallest of things to draw attention to what is greater.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 72:

﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾ The reference of "this" (hadhihi) is to the worldly life. The blindness here is intended as blindness of the heart: that is, whoever is blind to guidance in this world. "And he will be blind in the Hereafter" (fa-huwa fi yawm al-qiyamah a'mā): that is, bewildered and despairing of good. It is also possible that the blindness in the Hereafter is intended as blindness of sight, like His saying ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124]. The reason the blind one in the Hereafter is "more astray in the way" (adall sabilan) is that guidance will then not benefit him. The second "a'mā" may be an attributive adjective of the first, or it may be one of the elatives (af'al al-tafdil), and this is stronger, because of His saying "and more astray in the way," where adall, which is of the form af'al min kadha, is conjoined to what resembles it. Sibawayh said: it is not permissible to say "he is more blind than so-and-so," but this is prohibited only in blindness of sight, not in blindness of the heart.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 73–75:

﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Accept some of our affair and we will accept some of your affair." It is also said: the Thaqif asked the Prophet ﷺ to delay them for a year after their conversion, during which they would worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza. According to this report, the verse is Madani (revealed in Medina).

﴿That you should fabricate against Us other than it﴾. Here, al-iftira' (fabrication) is intended to mean opposing what was revealed to him of the Qur'an and other than it.

﴿And then they would have taken you as a close friend﴾. That is, if you had done what they wanted from you, they would have taken you as a close friend.

﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined toward them a little﴾. Law (lawla, "had it not been for") indicates the impossibility of one thing due to the existence of another. Here it indicates the impossibility of the Prophet ﷺ coming close to inclining toward them, owing to Allah's firming him and protecting him. Kada (almost/nearly) implies negation of the inclination, because the meaning of "so-and-so almost did such-and-such" is that he did not do it; thus the inclination toward them and coming close to it are negated. There is therefore no deficiency on the part of the Prophet ﷺ in this, because the firming prevented him from coming close to inclination. Had Allah not firmed him, his coming close to inclining toward them would have been "a little." As for the firming's effect, he did not incline at all, neither a little nor a lot, nor did he come close to that.

﴿Then We would have made you taste a double of life and a double of death﴾. That is, the punishment of both, had he done that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verses 76–77:

﴿And indeed, they almost tried to drive you out of the land﴾ The pronoun refers to the Quraysh, who had resolved to expel the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah; this was before the Hijrah. So "the land" here means Makkah, because it was his homeland. ﴿And if they had, they would not have remained after you except for a little while﴾ That is, had they expelled you, they would not have remained in Makkah after your departure except for a little while. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 78:

﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn.﴾ This verse is an indication of the obligatory prayers. "Dulūk al-shams" (the decline of the sun) is its zawāl (passing of its zenith), and it indicates the Ẓuhr (noon) and ʿAṣr (afternoon) prayers. "Ghasaq al-layl" is its darkness, and this indicates the Maghrib (sunset) and ʿIshāʾ (night) prayers. "Qurʾān al-fajr" is the Ṣubḥ (dawn) prayer. "Qurʾān al-fajr" is in the accusative by way of conjunction with the position of the lām in His words "li-dulūk al-shams," for the lām there is temporal, meaning "at" [sic]. It was also said: "It is a conjunction with al-ṣalāh (the prayer)." It was also said: it is an object of a hidden verb, its estimation being: "Recite the recitation of dawn." The prayer of Ṣubḥ was expressed as "the recitation of dawn" because the recitation (qurʾān) in it is more than in others, since it is performed with two long sūrahs. ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ That is, the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it, and they gather in it, for the angels of the night ascend and the angels of the day descend.

And from the night, keep vigil with it [as] a supererogatory [prayer] for you (﴿وَمِنَ ٱلْلَّيْلِ فَتَهَجَّدْ بِهِ نَافِلَةً لَّكَ﴾). When He commanded the obligatory acts (al-fara'id), He commanded the supererogatory acts (al-nawafil) after them. The particle "min" (من) here is for partitive meaning (li-l-tab'id), and the pronoun in "bihi" (به) refers to the Qur'an. Tahajjud (the night vigil prayer, from the root h-j-d) means staying awake, which is leaving off sleeping (al-hujud), and the meaning of hujud is sleep. The form tafa''ul (التفعل) here indicates departing from something, like taharruj (تحرج, avoiding what is straitened or wrongful) and ta'ththum (تأثم, avoiding sin), meaning leaving off sin and hardship.

﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ (﴿عَسَىٰ أَن يَبْعَثَكَ رَبُّكَ مَقَاماً مَّحْمُوداً﴾). It means intercession on the Day of Resurrection. The word "maqaman" (مقاماً) is in the accusative as an adverb of time/place (zarf).

﴿Say: My Lord, cause me to enter by a sincere entrance...﴾ (﴿وَقُل رَّبِّ أَدْخِلْنِي مُدْخَلَ صِدْقٍ﴾) up to the end of the verse. The "mudkhal" (entrance) is his entering Medina, and the "makhraj" (exit) is his leaving Mecca. It was also said that the entrance is into the grave and the exit is to the resurrection (al-ba'th). Ibn 'Atiyyah (ابن عطية) chose that it be general, covering all matters.

﴿...and grant me from Yourself an authority to help﴾ (﴿سُلْطَٰناً نَّصِيراً﴾). It was said: it means a proof (hujjah) by which You help me and through which my truthfulness is made manifest. It was also said: it means power and leadership by which You help me against the enemies. This second view is more apparent.

﴿And say: The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾. The truth is faith, and falsehood is disbelief.

﴿They ask you about the spirit.﴾ The askers were the Jews, though it was also said that they were the Quraysh, prompted by the Jews. The spirit (al-rūḥ) here, according to the majority (al-jumhūr, meaning the majority of scholars), is the one within the body, which is sometimes called the soul (al-nafs). It was also said that the spirit here is Gabriel, and that it is the Qur'an. The first view is the correct one, because what follows indicates it.

﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord.﴾ That is, it is among the matters that God has kept to Himself and has not disclosed to His creation. The Jews had told the Quraysh, "Ask him about the spirit. If he does not give you an answer about it, then he is a prophet." This was because they had in the Torah that the spirit is among the things whose knowledge God alone possesses (the Torah, al-Tawrah). Ibn Buraydah said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed away without knowing the spirit. People have greatly differed about the soul and the spirit, and there is nothing in their statements on this that can be relied upon."

﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾ This is a general address to all people, because their knowledge is little compared with the knowledge of God. It was also said that it is addressed to the Jews specifically, but the first view is clearer, because it points to the fact that they cannot attain knowledge of the spirit.

﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you.﴾ That is, if We willed, We could take away the Qur'an, erasing it from the chests (of men) and from the codices (al-maṣāḥif). This verse is connected in meaning to His saying: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little." That is, it is within Our power to take away what We revealed to you, so that no knowledge would remain with you.

﴿Then you would find for yourself therefrom no advocate against Us.﴾ That is, no one who would take responsibility for restoring it and returning it after it has been taken away.

﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord.﴾ This may be a contiguous exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), so the meaning is that the mercy of your Lord would return the Qur'an after its removal, if it were removed. Or it may be a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning that the mercy of your Lord holds it back from being taken away.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 88:

﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce the like of it, even if they were helpers to one another.﴾ The inability of later generations to produce its like is due to what it contains of divine sciences, clear proofs, and wondrous meanings that people did not know and could not reach, and which it presents in complete form. Most people said: they were unable to produce it because of its eloquence (fasahah) and the excellence of its composition (husn nazm). Its aspects of inimitability (i'jaz) are many; I have mentioned fifteen of them elsewhere. ﴿ظَهِيراً﴾ means "helper" (mu'in).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 89–92:

﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾. That is, We have made clear to them everything of beneficial knowledge, established proofs, and clear arguments. This shows that the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an lies in its meanings and sciences, as we have mentioned. ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾. Al-kufur: denial (al-judud). It is put in the accusative by his saying "abā" (refused) because it carries the sense of negation. ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring"﴾. Those who said this statement were the nobles of Quraysh, who asked the Prophet ﷺ for various kinds of extraordinary feats (kharq al-adah), which are those mentioned by God in this verse. It is said that the one who said it was Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah, who was a cousin of the Prophet ﷺ on his aunt's side, and who later embraced Islam. Al-yanbu' is a spring. They said to him: "Mecca is short of water, so cause a spring of water to gush forth for us in it." ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾. This is a reference to God's saying: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall drop upon them pieces from the sky﴾ [Saba': 9]. Kisafan with a fatha on the sin is the plural of kisfah, which means a piece; it is also read with a sukun, meaning a single piece. ﴿Qabilan﴾. It is said its meaning is "confrontation and direct witnessing." It is also said: "a guarantor, a witness to your truthfulness." And al-qabalah in the language means guarantee.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 97:**

﴿Blind, dumb, and deaf﴾. It has been said: this is a metaphor, meaning that on the Day of Resurrection they will be bewildered (ḥayārā). It has also been said: it is literal, and that they will be blind, dumb, and deaf at the moment they rise from their graves. ﴿Whenever it subsides﴾: its meaning linguistically is that its flame has calmed (sakana lahabuhā). Here the intended meaning is: whenever their flesh is consumed and its flame subsides, they are given other bodies (ajsādan ukhar), and then it blazes again, more intensely than it was before.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 17, verses 98–99:**

﴿And they say: "When we have become bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be raised up as a new creation?"﴾ This is a expression of disbelief in the resurrection (al-hashr, the gathering of creation for judgment). The meaning of *rufat* (crumbled dust) has already been explained, and the discussion of the two interrogatives (al-istifhamayn, the two questions in the verse) has also been covered.

﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them?﴾ This is an argument for the resurrection. The heavens and the earth are greater than the human being. Since Allah has the power to create them, it is more fitting and more certain that He has the power to restore the human body after its annihilation. The "seeing" in the verse is seeing with the heart (ru'yat qalb), i.e., understanding and reflection.

﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt.﴾ This term is either the Day of Resurrection or the appointed time of death.

﴿Say: "If you were to possess﴾ "Law" (law, a conditional particle expressing the non-occurrence of the consequent because of the non-occurrence of the condition) is a particle of imtina' (negation of consequence). A verb may follow it only if it is explicit or implicit, so a verb must be supposed here after it. Its estimated form is "you possess," and then it is explained by the explicit "tamlikun" (you possess). "Antum" (you) is an emphatic for the pronoun in the implicit "tamlikun."

﴿the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord﴾ That is, the wealth and the provisions.

﴿Then you would surely withhold, for fear of spending﴾ That is, if you possessed the treasuries, you would withhold giving out of fear of poverty. So "spending" here means the consequence of spending, which is poverty. The object of "amsaktum" (you withheld) is omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it has no object, because its meaning is "you were stingy," from their saying of the miser, "mimsik" (a withholder).

The meaning of the verse is a description of man as miserly and fearful of poverty, in contrast with the description of God, the Exalted, as generous and self-sufficient.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 101–102:

﴿Nine clear signs﴾ (tis'a ayat bayyinat). Five of them were the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood; and the four were the staff turning into a serpent, his hand coming out white, the untying of the knot from his tongue, and the splitting of the sea. In them was also the promise of lifting the Mount (al-Tur) above them, and the water gushing from the rock, so that two of them fall away from the other. In them was also (the promise of) the years of drought and the lack of fruits. It is narrated that some of the Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about them, and he said: "Do not associate anything with Allah, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not walk with an innocent person to the ruler so that he may kill him, do not practise sorcery, do not consume usury, do not slander chaste women, do not flee on the day of the advancing battle; and upon you, specifically the Jews, (is) not to transgress on the Sabbath."

﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾ (fa-su'al Bani Isra'il), i.e., ask those contemporaries of yours from the Children of Israel about what we have mentioned of the story of Musa, so that you may increase in certainty. The verse according to this is an address to Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, "We said to Musa: ask the Children of Israel from Pharaoh," i.e., request from him that he send them with you, so it is like His saying: "that you send with us the Children of Israel." Thus His saying "ask" is not to Musa with the implied "say." He also said: it may mean: "ask the Children of Israel to support you and to be with you," and this is also on the basis that the address is to Musa. The first is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 17, verse 110:

﴿Say: "Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)."﴾ The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers heard the Prophet (ﷺ) calling, "O Allah, O Merciful (Ya Rahman)." They said, "If Muhammad commands us to call upon one God, then here he is calling upon two." So the verse was revealed to make clear that his saying "Allah" or "al-Rahman" is a name for one and the same Named Being, and that one is free to call upon Him by whichever of the two names one wishes. The word "call" (*ad'u*) in the verse means "naming," as in your saying, "I named my son Zayd," not "calling out" (*al-nida'*).

﴿Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ *Ayyan* is a conditional noun (*ism shart*) in the accusative, governed by *tad'u*. The tanwin (*al-tanwin*) on it is a substitute (*'iwad*) for the genitive noun it would have been followed by. *Ma* (*ma*) is an extra particle added for emphasis. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to Allah, the Named Being. The meaning is: whichever of these two names you call upon, it is good, because Allah has the most beautiful names. Thus the phrase *lahu al-asma' al-husna* ("to Him belong the most beautiful names") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*mawdi' al-hal*), and in meaning it gives the reason for the answer: since all His names are beautiful, these two names are beautiful too.

﴿And do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor be silent in it.﴾ *Al-mukhafatah* (the lowering of the voice, i.e. silent recitation) is *al-israr* (speaking in a whisper). The occasion of the verse was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an aloud in the prayer, and the polytheists heard it, so they reviled the Qur'an and the One who sent it down. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was then commanded to take a middle course between whispering and loud recitation, so that his companions who prayed with him could hear, while the polytheists would not. It was also said: the meaning is, do not raise your voice in all of your prayer, and do not whisper all of it, but make part of it silent and part of it aloud, as the Sunnah has established. It was also said: "prayer" (*al-salah*) here means supplication (*al-du'a'*).
